embedded_source: Probably from factor + -y, although in noun sense 1 (“a place where manufacturing takes place”) apparently influenced strongly by association with Classical Latin fact-, the past participial stem of faciō (“to make”); compare manufactory and Latin factōrium (“an oil press”). embedded_source: From Middle English pyne, from Old English *pīne, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā, from Latin pīnus, see there for more. Doublet of pinus. Possibly related to fat.

note: ラテン語 pausare（止まる）から（後に ponere「置く」と混同された）。ある姿勢で止まる →「ポーズ（をとる）・（問題を）提起する」。
embedded_source: From Middle English pose, from Old English ġeposu pl (“cold in the head; catarrh”, literally “(the) sneezes; (the) snorts”), from Old English pos, ġepos (“sneeze, snort”), from Proto-West Germanic *pos, from Proto-Germanic *pusą (“sneeze, snort”), from Proto-Germanic *pusōną, *pusjaną (“to snort, blow”), from *pus- (“to blow, breathe hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“to blow, swell”). Compare Low German pusten (“to blow, puff”), German dialectal pfausen (“to sneeze, snort”), Norwegian dialectal pysa (“to blow”).

embedded_source: From Latin diārium (“a daily allowance for soldiers, in Late Latin also ‘diary’”), neuter of *diārius, from diēs (“a day”) (whence also journal). Cognate with Spanish diario (“daily; diary”).

note: dis（否定）+ agree（同意する）。「意見が合わない」。
embedded_source: From Middle English disagre (“to refuse to assent to”), from Anglo-Norman disagreer, disagrer, desagreer (“to refuse assent”), from Old French desagreer, desagrëer (“to be disagreeable; to be unpleasant”) (modern French désagréer (“to displease”)); the English word is analysable as dis- + agree.

embedded_source: From Gene(s) (also spelled Jean(s)), an obsolete English name for the Italian city of Genoa. Compare French Gênes. In the context of clothing, the term originally denoted a kind of coarse cotton (known more fully as Gene(s) fustian) that was associated with Genoa. It began to be used for trousers made of such cloth in the 19th century. At this point, the final -s was reanalysed as a plural ending.

Related also to Old English leċċan (“to water, wet”), Albanian lag, lak (“to damp, make wet”). See also leach, lake.

Cognate with Scots sok (“sock, stocking”), West Frisian sok (“sock”), Dutch sok (“sock”), German Socke (“sock”), Danish sok, sokke (“sock”), Swedish sock, socka (“sock”), Icelandic sokkur (“sock”). Doublet of zocco; also related to zoccolo, socle, and zocalo.

Perhaps imitative, related to bump, or related to Middle English bonchen (“to pound, beat”) and Dutch bonken (“to bump”).\nCompare Saterland Frisian bumzje (“to pound, bang, bounce”), West Frisian bûnzje (“to throb, bounce, pulsate”), Dutch bonzen (“to thump, knock, throb, bounce”), German Low German bunsen, bumsen (“to beat, bounce”), German bumsen (“to thud, bang, pound”).

embedded_source: The verb is from Middle English ferien (“to carry, convey”), from Old English ferian, from Proto-West Germanic *farjan, from Proto-Germanic *farjaną, which see for cognates. This verb is the causative of Proto-Germanic *faraną (“to go, travel”), whence English fare; ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *per-.\nThe noun is from Middle English ferie (“place of crossing, ferry”), which was derived from the above verb under influence of Old Norse ferja, from Proto-Germanic *farjǭ, itself also from the verb.\nFalse cognate of Latin ferō.

embedded_source: From Middle English fischer, fischare, from Old English fisċere (“fisher”), from Proto-Germanic *fiskārijaz (“fisher”), equivalent to fish + -er. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Fisker (“fisher”), West Frisian fisker (“fisher”), Dutch visser (“fisher”), German Low German Fisker, Fisser (“fisher”), German Fischer (“fisher”), Danish fisker (“fisher”), Swedish fiskare (“fisher”).

note: flex（曲げる）+ ibility。曲げられる性質 →「柔軟性」。
embedded_source: From French flexibilité, from Late Latin flexibilitās, from Latin flectō (“to bend, curve”). Equivalent to flexible + -ity = flex + -ibility.

note: refrigerator を短くした語。re（再び）+ frigus（寒さ）。frigid（極寒の）。
embedded_source: The noun is a clipping of refrigerator, perhaps influenced by the Frigidaire brand of refrigerators, or frigerator (“(dated) refrigerator”). The spelling is likely influenced by analogy with bridge, ridge, etc. The verb is derived from the noun.\nThe fandom slang verb sense alludes to the phrase "women in refrigerators" coined by the American comic book writer Gail Simone. Simone was referencing a plot point in Green Lantern (volume 3, issue 54, 1994), in which the Green Lantern's girlfriend is murdered by a villain, and her body placed in a refrigerator for him to find.

note: ラテン語 fundere（注ぐ・溶かす）から。fus + ion。溶けて一つになること →「融合・核融合」。
embedded_source: First appears c. 1555, in a translation by Richard Eden. From Middle French fusion, from Latin fūsiōnem (the accusative of fūsiō), from fusus, past participle of fundō (“to pour; to melt”) (see also found). Doublet of foison.

embedded_source: From Middle English gauge, gaugen, from Anglo-Norman, Old Northern French gauger (compare Modern French jauger from Old French jaugier), from gauge (“gauging rod”), from Frankish *galgā (“measuring rod, pole”), from Proto-Germanic *galgô (“pole, stake, cross”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰalgʰ-, *ǵʰalg- (“perch, long switch”). Cognate with Old High German galgo, Old Frisian galga, Old English ġealga (“cross-beam, gallows”), Old Norse galgi (“cross-beam, gallows”), Old Norse gelgja (“pole, perch”). Doublet of gallows.

note: 古英語 gāt から。北欧語・ドイツ語 Geiß と同じゲルマン系の語。
embedded_source: Inherited from Middle English goot, got, gat, from Old English gāt, from Proto-West Germanic *gait, from Proto-Germanic *gaits, from a substrate language.\nThe sense of lecherous man derives from the slang expression “horny as a goat”.

note: 古英語 guttas（腸）から。「腸」→（guts）「根性」→「直感的な」（gut feeling）。

Related to English gote (“drain”), Old English ġēotan (“to pour”). More at gote, yote.\nThe verb is from Middle English gutten, gotten (“to gut”).

The Old French is itself of Germanic origin (whence Old English helm). Used in English since the 15th century, it has largely displaced helm as the general word.

Modern sense of “doctrine” attributed to use of related idéologue (“ideologue”) by Napoleon Bonaparte as a term of abuse towards political opponents in early 1800s.

embedded_source: A calque of German Übermensch; super- + man. embedded_source: Probably from Middle English yerk (“sudden motion”) and Middle English yerkid (“tightly pulled”), from Old English ġearc (“ready, active, quick”) and Old English ġearcian (“to prepare, make ready, procure, furnish, supply”). note: オランダ語 loterij から。lot（くじ・分け前）+ -ery。a lot of（たくさん）の lot も「くじで分けた分け前」から。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Italian lotteria, from the same root as Old English hlot (cognate with English lot). Compare French loterie (from Middle Dutch loterie). By surface analysis, lot + -ery.

note: ラテン語 magnus（大きい）から。「大きさ・規模」。magnify（拡大する）、magnificent も同じ。
embedded_source: From Latin magnitūdō (“greatness, size”), magnus + -tūdō.

note: ラテン語 minus（より少なく）から。min（小さい）。→「マイナス・〜を引いた」。
embedded_source: From Middle English mynus, from Latin minus, neuter form of minor, comparative form of parvus (“small, little”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *mey- (“few, small”).

note: ラテン語 nudus（裸の）から。naked と同系の印欧祖語にさかのぼる。
embedded_source: Entered English 1493 as a legal term, meaning "unsupported, not formally attested," from Middle English nud, from Latin nūdus (“naked, bare”).

note: out（外へ）+ let（行かせる）。「外へ出す口」→「出口・はけ口・コンセント・販売店」。
embedded_source: From Middle English outlete, outeleate, ut-lete, derived from Middle English outleten (“to allow, let out, emit”), equivalent to out- + let. Compare West Frisian útlit (“outlet”), Dutch uitlaat (“outlet”), German Auslass (“outlet”).

note: para（そばに）+ meter（測る）。補助として測るもの →「媒介変数・条件・範囲」。
embedded_source: From French paramètre, from New Latin parametrum (“parameter”), from Ancient Greek παρα- (para-, “beside”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”).

note: ギリシャ語 pausis（停止）から。pauein（止める）。「止まること」→「休止」。
embedded_source: From Middle French pause, from Latin pausa, from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis), from Ancient Greek παύω (paúō, “stop”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of pausa.

note: 古フランス語 plege（保証人・担保）から。「担保を差し出して約束する」→「誓約・公約」。
embedded_source: From Middle English plege, from Anglo-Norman plege, from Old French plege (Modern French pleige) from Medieval Latin plevium, plebium, from plebiō (“to pledge”), from Frankish *plehan (“to pledge; to support; to guarantee”). Akin to Old High German pflegan (“to take care of, be accustomed to”), Old Saxon plegan (“to vouch for”), Old English plēon (“to risk, endanger”). More at plight.

note: ラテン語 porta（門）から。→「（立派な）入口・玄関・ポータルサイト」。port（港）と同じ祖先。
embedded_source: From Middle English portal, porttol, from Old French portal and Medieval Latin portāle, from porta.

embedded_source: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French prescripcion, from Latin praescriptio (“preface; pretext; something written ahead of time”), from prae- (“pre-, before”) + scribere (“to write”) + -tio (“-tion, forming nouns”). Equivalent to prescribe + -tion.

embedded_source: From French publicité, From Medieval Latin pūblicitātem, accusative singular of pūblicitās, from Latin pūblicus (“public, general”). Morphologically public + -ity.

embedded_source: Borrowed from French télégraphe, equivalent to tele- (“far, distant”) + -graph (“writing”), suggested as a new name for Claude Chappe's overland semaphore network by André François Miot de Mélito in place of Chappe's original tachygraphe (“tachygraph, fast writer”).

note: ラテン語 vacca（牛）から。牛痘（牛の天然痘）を使った種痘から名づけられた。
embedded_source: Learned borrowing from Latin vaccīnus (“of or derived from a cow”), from vacca (“cow (female cattle)”) + -īnus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Sense 1 refers to the early use of the cowpox virus as a vaccination against smallpox: see New Latin variolae vaccīnae (“cowpox”, plural, literally “infectious diseases of cattle causing pustules”), coined by the British physician and scientist Edward Jenner (1749–1823).

embedded_source: From Middle English barn, bern, bærn, from Old English bearn, bern, contracted forms of Old English berern, bereærn (“barn, granary”), compound of bere (“barley”) and ærn, ræn (“dwelling, barn”), from Proto-West Germanic *raʀn, from Proto-Germanic *razną (compare Old Norse rann), from pre-Germanic *h₁rh̥₁-s-nó-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erh₁- (“to rest”).\nMore at rest and barley.\nFor the use as a unit of surface area, see w:Barn (unit) § Etymology.

embedded_source: From Middle English cathedral, chathedral, cathiderall, from Old French [Term?], from Latin cathedrālis, from cathedra + -ālis, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra, “chair of a teacher, throne”).

note: ラテン語 claudere（閉じる）から。「区切られた（閉じた）一まとまり」→「節・条項」。close、include も同じ。
embedded_source: From Middle English clause, claus, borrowed from Old French clause, from Medieval Latin clausa (Latin diminutive clausula (“close, end; a clause, close of a period”)), from Latin clausus, past participle of claudere (“to shut, close”). See close, its doublet.

The English word is probably a doublet of clot.
The verb is derived from the noun.

note: ギリシャ語 kylindros（転がるもの）から。kylindein（転がす）。「転がる筒」→「円柱・シリンダー」。
embedded_source: From Middle French chilindre, cylindre, from Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros), from κυλίνδω (kulíndō) "I roll or wallow" (intransitive). Doublet of calander and calender.

embedded_source: From Middle English dauncer, dawncere, dancere, equivalent to dance + -er.

note: 古英語 dēaf から。ドイツ語 taub と同じ。「ぼんやりした・感覚が鈍い」が原義とされる。
embedded_source: From Middle English def, deef, from Old English dēaf, from Proto-West Germanic *daub (“deaf”), from Proto-Germanic *daubaz (“deaf or stunned”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, smoke, darken, obscure”). Cognate with Ancient Greek τυφλός (tuphlós, “blind”). See also dumb. Doublet of daff, dof, and dowf.\nCognate with Dutch doof, German taub, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål døv, Norwegian Nynorsk dauv, Swedish döv, Faroese deyvur, Icelandic daufur.

embedded_source: From Middle English dokke, from Old English docce, from Proto-West Germanic *dokkā, from Proto-Germanic *dukkǭ (compare Old Danish dokke (“water-dock”), West Flemish dokke, dokkebladeren (“coltsfoot, butterbur”)), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew- (“dark”) (compare Latvian duga (“scum, slime on water”)).

note: フランス語 entreprendre（企てる）から。entre（間に）+ prendre（取る）。「手に取って引き受ける人」→「起業家」。enterprise と同じ。
embedded_source: Borrowed from French entrepreneur (“one who undertakes or manages”), from Middle French entrepreneur, from entreprendre (“to undertake”) + -eur.

note: e（外へ・はっきり）+ vid（見る）+ ent。はっきり見える →「明白な」。evidence（証拠）。
embedded_source: From Middle English evident, from Old French evident, from Latin ēvidēns (“visible, apparent, clear, plain”) (compare Late Latin ēvideor (“to appear plainly”)), from ē (“out”) + videō (“see”), present participle vidēns, deponent videor (“to appear, seem”). Displaced native Old English sweotol.

embedded_source: From Middle French expédition, and its source, Latin expeditio.

embedded_source: Anglicisation of French faciliter (“facilitate”) through -ate (verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Latin facilis.

embedded_source: From Middle English honeste (“honour, integrity”), from Old French honesté (compare modern French honnêteté). By surface analysis, honest + -y. Displaced native Old English sōþfæstnes and non-native Middle English prodonomee, from Old French prodomie. The plant is named so after the visibility of the seeds through the translucent pods.

embedded_source: Inherited from Middle English infaunt, borrowed from Latin īnfantem, accusative masculine singular of īnfāns, nominal use of the adjective meaning 'not able to speak', from īn- (“not”) + fāns, present participle of for (“to speak”). note: in（中へ）+ it（行く）+ iate。中へ入らせる →「始める・入会させる」。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Latin initiātus, perfect passive participle of initiō (“to begin, originate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from initium (“a beginning”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from initus (“an entrance, coming in, approach”) + -ium, from ineō + -tus, from in- + eō (“to go”). Cognate with French initier.

note: instrument（道具）+ al。道具となる →「助けになる・器楽の」。
embedded_source: From Middle English instrumental, instrumentale, from Medieval Latin īnstrūmentālis, equivalent to instrument + -al.

embedded_source: The verb is derived from Middle French insulter (modern French insulter (“to insult”)) or its etymon Latin īnsultō (“to spring, leap or jump at or upon; to abuse, insult, revile, taunt”), the frequentative form of īnsiliō (“to bound; to leap in or upon”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside, within’) + saliō (“to bound, jump, leap; to spring forth; to flow down”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“to spring”)).\nThe noun is derived from Middle French insult (modern French insulte (“insult”)) or its etymon Late Latin insultus (“insult, reviling, scoffing”), from īnsiliō (“to bound; to

note: interfere（干渉する）+ -ence。inter（間）+ ferire（打つ）。「間に入って打つ」→「干渉・妨害」。
embedded_source: From interfere + -ence. The sense in physics was likely introduced by English polymath Thomas Young, which he used as early as 1801 in a paper in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society.

embedded_source: From Middle French coordination, from Late Latin coōrdinātiōnem (accusative of coōrdinātiō), from con- + ōrdinātiō. Morphologically coordinate + -ion.

note: dis（離れて）+ cret（ふるい分ける）+ ion。見分ける力 →「判断の自由・分別・慎重さ」。
embedded_source: From Middle English discrecioun, from Old French discretion, from Late Latin discrētiō, from Latin discerno. Equivalent to discreet + -ion.

embedded_source: From Middle English historian, historien, from Old French historien, from Latin historia (“story, history”), equivalent to histor(y) + -ian. More at history.

embedded_source: Borrowed from Middle French horizontal, from horizon, horizonte, from Latin horizōn (stem horizont-).

note: ラテン語 hospes（客・もてなす人）から。hospital（客をもてなす所 → 病院）、host、hotel も同じ。
embedded_source: From Middle English hospitalite, from Old French hospitalité (modern French hospitalité), from Latin hospitālitās (“hospitality”), from hospitālis (“hospitable”), from hospes (“guest", "host”). Displaced native Old English cumlīþnes (literally “guest gentleness”).

note: 古フランス語 ostage（人質）から。ラテン語 obses（人質）とされるが、host（もてなす人）の影響も受けた。

Displaced native Old English ġīsl.

embedded_source: From Latin pharmaceuticus (“of drugs”) + -al, from Ancient Greek φαρμακευτικός (pharmakeutikós, “of or by means of drugs or pharmacy”).

embedded_source: From Old French coral (French corail), from Latin corallium, from Ancient Greek κοράλλιον (korállion, “coral”). note: ギリシャ神話で天を担ぐ巨人アトラス（Atlas）から。16世紀の地図帳の表紙にアトラスが描かれたことから「地図帳」。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Latin Atlas, from the name of the Ancient Greek mythological figure Ἄτλας (Átlas, “Bearer (of the Heavens)”), from τλῆναι (tlênai, “to suffer”, “to endure”, “to bear”). The sense referring to books of maps comes from the Atlas of Mercator, which he named thus in honor of Atlas, who was supposed to be skillful in astronomy and the doctrine of the sphere. The sense referring to the vertebra reflects that the spine carries the globe of the cranium (the neck carries the head).

embedded_source: From bi- + -sexual, via the French bisexuel (bi-, sexuel). Attested since 1792 as a synonym in botany for "hermaphroditic" ("having male and female parts"). First used of sexuality in Richard von Krafft-Ebing's 1886 Psychopathia Sexualis (in German) and Charles Gilbert Chaddock's 1892 English translation thereof, due to the theory that people were naturally attracted to the opposite sex and so the brain or mind of a person attracted to "both" sexes (or to the same sex) must be partly of another sex and thus "hermaphroditic".

From Middle English loppestere, lopster, from Old English loppestre, lopustre, lopystre, of uncertain origin. Some believe it to be a corruption of Latin lō̆custa (“grasshopper, locust”) + the Old English feminine agent suffix -estre. embedded_source: From Middle French erosion, from Latin ērōsiō (“eating away”), derived from ērōdō.\nThe first known occurrence in English was in the 1541 translation by Robert Copland of Guy de Chauliac's medical text The Questyonary of Cyrurygens. Copland used erosion to describe how ulcers developed in the mouth. By 1774 erosion was used outside medical subjects. Oliver Goldsmith employed the term in the more contemporary geological context, in his book Natural History, with the quote\n: "Bounds are thus put to the erosion of the earth by water."

embedded_source: From Middle French manœuvre (“manipulation, maneuver”) and manouvrer (“to maneuver”), from Old French manovre (“handwork, manual labor”), from Medieval Latin manopera, manuopera (“work done by hand, handwork”), from manu (“by hand”) + operari (“to work”). note: medicine + -al。「薬効のある」。

embedded_source: From the past participle of nim (“to take”). Compare German benommen (“dazed, numb”) and Old Norse numinn. The final ⟨b⟩ is a later addition; it was never pronounced, and did not appear in the original word.

embedded_source: From Middle English paun, pawyn, pawnd, from Old French pan, pant (“pledge for a payment”), from a Germanic language, perhaps Frankish *pand (“deposit, security, pledge”), further origin uncertain. embedded_source: From Middle English sanite, sanyte, sanytee, from Middle French sanité, from Latin sānitās, from sānus (“healthy”) + -itās (“-ity”). By surface analysis, sane + -ity.

embedded_source: Originally the same word as scuffle, and properly a frequentative of shove.

See also Norwegian sleip (“slippery”) and Icelandic sleipur.

embedded_source: From Middle English traunce, from Anglo-Norman transe (“fear of coming evil; passage from life to death”), from transir (“to be numb with fear; to die, pass on”), from Latin trānseō (“to cross over”).

note: ギリシャ語 anthos（花）+ logia（集めること）。「花を摘み集めたもの」→「選集」。chrysanthemum（金の花 → 菊）と同じ anth。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνθολογία (anthología, “flower-gathering”), from ἀνθολογέω (anthologéō, “I gather flowers”), from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”) + λέγω (légō, “I gather, pick up, collect”), coined by Meleager of Gadara circa 60 BCE, originally as Στέφανος (στέφανος (stéphanos, “garland”)) to describe a collection of poetry, later retitled anthology – see Greek Anthology. Anthologiai were collections of small Greek poems and epigrams, because in Greek culture the flower symbolized the finer sentiments that only poetry can express. By surface analysis, antho- + -logy.

note: ラテン語 auditor（聞く人）から。audire（聞く）。昔は帳簿を読み上げて聞いて確かめたことから「監査役」。audio と同じ。
embedded_source: From Anglo-Norman auditour, from Latin audītor (“hearer, auditor”).

note: スイスのフランス語 lavanche が avaler（下る）の影響で変化した語。「雪崩」→「殺到」。
embedded_source: From French avalanche, from Franco-Provençal (Savoy) avalançhe, blend of aval (“downhill”) and standard lavençhe, from Vulgar Latin *labanka (compare Occitan lavanca, Italian valanga), of uncertain origin, perhaps an alteration of Late Latin lābīna (“landslide”) (compare Franco-Provençal (Dauphiné) lavino, Romansh lavina), from Latin lābēs, from lābor (“to slip, slide”).

note: 語源ははっきりしない。badge（顔の白い印）と関係するとされる。犬にアナグマを追わせた遊びから「しつこくせがむ」。
embedded_source: From Middle English bageard (“marked by a badge”), from bage (“badge”), referring to the animal's badge-like white blaze, equivalent to badge + -ard. Displaced earlier brock, from Old English brocc.

note: 語源ははっきりしない。17世紀のロンドンの俗語。「冗談のやりとり」。
embedded_source: 1670s as verb, 1680s as noun. The origin is unknown, possibly from London street slang; ostensibly as *bant + -er (frequentative suffix). Possibly an Anglo-Gaelicism from the Irish bean (“woman”), so that "banter" means "talk of women."

note: bid（入札する）+ -er。「入札者」。
embedded_source: From Middle English bidder, biddere, equivalent to bid + -er. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Bidder, German Bitter.

note: block（街区）+ buster（壊すもの）。第二次大戦で街区ごと吹き飛ばす爆弾 →「大ヒット作」。
embedded_source: From block + buster, referring originally to aerial bombs capable of destroying a whole block of buildings.

note: blue（青）+ print（印刷）。昔の設計図が青焼きだったことから「青写真・設計図」。
embedded_source: From blue + print. Introduced by Sir John Herschel in 1842.

note: bowl（ボールを投げる）+ -er。「投手・ボウリングをする人」。帽子の bowler は帽子屋の名から。
embedded_source: From bowl + -er.

note: イタリア語 cammeo から。語源ははっきりしない。小さく浮き彫りにした肖像 →「（有名人の）ちょい役」。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Italian cammeo, from Medieval Latin camaeus, of unknown origin. The movie sense is short for “cameo role” referring to a famous person who was playing no character, but him or herself. Like a cameo brooch — a low-relief carving of a person’s head or bust — the actor or celebrity is instantly recognizable. More recently, it has come to refer to any short appearances, whether as a character or as oneself. Doublet of camaieu.

note: スペイン語 caramelo から。ラテン語 calamellus（小さな葦）とされる。
embedded_source: Borrowed from French caramel, from Spanish caramelo, from Portuguese caramelo, dissimilated from Late Latin calamellus, diminutive of calamus (“reed”) (and a doublet of chalumeau and shawm). Alternatively from Medieval Latin cannamellis, which is a compound of canna + mellis.

note: charisma（カリスマ）+ -tic。ギリシャ語 kharisma（恵み・賜物）。「神から授かった魅力のある」。
embedded_source: From Ancient Greek χάρισμα (khárisma, “grace, favour, gift”) + -ic.

note: ギリシャ語 khrōma（色）+ sōma（体）。染料でよく染まる体 →「染色体」。chrome（クロム）と同じ。
embedded_source: 19th century: from German Chromosom, ultimately from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour”) + σῶμα (sôma, “body”) (because they are stained under the microscope). Equivalent to chromo- + -some.

note: commence（始まる）+ -ment。「開始」→ 社会人生活の始まり →（米）「卒業式」。
embedded_source: From French commencement; analyzable as commence + -ment.

note: ラテン語 confiscare（国庫に入れる）から。con + fiscus（かご・国庫）。fiscal（財政の）と同じ。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Latin cōnfiscātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin cōnfiscō (“to seize for the public treasury (fiscus)”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

note: contradict（矛盾する）+ -ory。contra（反対に）+ dicere（言う）。「矛盾した」。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Late Latin contradictorius, from Latin contradico. Equivalent to contradict + -ory.

note: ラテン語 conventus（集会）から。convenire（集まる）。「修道会」→「女子修道院」。convention と同じ ven。
embedded_source: From Middle English convent, variant of covent, from Old French covent, from Latin conventus, perfect participle of the verb convenio (whence ultimately convene), see con- + venio. Doublet of coven.

note: con（共に）+ vers（向ける）+ e。互いに向き合う →「会話する」、向きが逆の →「逆（の）」。
embedded_source: From Old French converser, from Latin conversor (“live, have dealings with”).

embedded_source: From Middle English corrosioun, from Old French corrosion, or its source, Late Latin corrōsiōnem, accusative singular of corrōsiō (“gnawing away, corroding”), from Latin corrōdō (“gnaw away, corrode”).

dear + -ly。「心から」→「高い代価を払って」（dear の「高価な」の意味から）。

embedded_source: From Middle English disposicioun, from Middle French disposition, from Latin dispositiōnem, accusative singular of dispositiō, from dispōnō. By surface analysis, dispose + -ition. Doublet of dispositio.

note: ギリシャ語 ekstasis（自分の外に立つこと）＝ ek + histanai（立つ）。「我を忘れること」→「恍惚」。
embedded_source: From Old French estaise (“ecstasy, rapture”), from Latin ecstasis, from Ancient Greek ἔκστασις (ékstasis), from ἐξίστημι (exístēmi, “to displace”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

note: eighteen + -th。「18番目」。
embedded_source: Inherited from Middle English eightetenthe, eightetethe, from Old English eahtatēoþa, from Proto-Germanic *ahtudô tehundô. Equivalent to eighteen + -th (ordinal suffix).

note: eleven + -th。「11番目」。eleven は「（10を数えて）1つ残る」の意。
embedded_source: From Middle English elleventhe, from elleven + -the, equivalent to eleven + -th. This re-formation replaced inherited forms such as ellefte, enlefte, from Old English endlefta, from Proto-Germanic *ainaliftô.

note: フランス語 envoyer（送る）から。ラテン語 inviare（道に送り出す）、via（道）。「使節」。
embedded_source: From French envoyé (“envoy, messenger”), from envoyer (“send”).

note: fabricate（作る・でっち上げる）+ -ion。ラテン語 fabrica（作業場）。「製造・でっち上げ」。
embedded_source: From Middle French fabrication, from Latin fabricatio. Equivalent to fabricate + -ion.

note: fascinate（魅了する）+ -ion。ラテン語 fascinare（魔法をかける）。「魅了」。
embedded_source: From Latin fascinare ("to bewitch"), possibly from Ancient Greek βασκαίνιεν (baskaínien, “to speak ill of; to curse”). Morphologically fascinate + -ion.

note: 古英語 fyrh から。「モミ」。

From Middle English firre, from Old English fyrh, furh, as in furhwudu (“pinewood”), from Proto-West Germanic *furhu, from Proto-Germanic *furhō, *furhijǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *pŕ̥kʷeh₂, from *pérkʷus (“oak”). Possibly conflated during Middle English with Old Norse fýri (as in fýriskógr (“pine-wood”).
Germanic cognates include Dutch vuren, Low German Fuhr, German Föhre (“pine”), Danish fyr). Outside of Germanic, compare Italian (Trentino) porca

note: formulate（定式化する）+ -ion。ラテン語 formula（小さな型）、forma。「策定・配合」。
中世ラテン語 Francorum rex（フランク人の王）と刻まれた硬貨から。「フラン」。France、frank と同じ。
embedded_source: Borrowed from French franc. Doublet of Frank, frank, and farang.

note: front + -al。「正面の」→「前頭の」（frontal lobe：前頭葉）。
embedded_source: Borrowed from New Latin frontālis, from frons (“the forehead, brow, front”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent to front + -al; cognate of French frontal. Doublet of frontalis.

note: goalkeeper の短縮。
embedded_source: Clipping of goalkeeper or goaltender + -ie.

note: ラテン語 gradi（歩む）の現在分詞。「段階的に変わるもの」→「勾配・グラデーション」。grade、graduate と同じ grad。
embedded_source: From Latin gradiēns, present participle of gradior (“to step, to walk”).

note: 古フランス語 grané（穀粒で味つけしたソース）の写し間違いとされる。「肉汁ソース」。
embedded_source: From Middle English gravey, greavie, gravy; probably from greaves, graves (“the sediment of melted tallow”), or from Old French grave, a claimed misspelling of grané (“stew, spice”), from grain (“spice”).\nSense of "pasta sauce" apparently seems to be from Italian dialect, especially Calabrian, differentiating tomato puree (salsa (“sauce”)) from cooked tomato sauce (sugo).

note: 古英語 hǣring から。「ニシン」。red herring（燻製ニシン）は猟犬の訓練でにおいをそらすのに使ったことから「人の気をそらすもの」。
embedded_source: From Middle English hering, from Old English hǣring, from Proto-West Germanic *hāring (“herring”), further etymology unknown. Possibly derived from Proto-Germanic *hērą (“hair”) + -ing, due to the similarity of their fine bones to hair. Cognate with Scots hering, haring (“herring”), Saterland Frisian Hiering, Häiring (“herring”), West Frisian hjerring (“herring”), Dutch haring (“herring”), German Low German Hereng, Hering (“herring”), German Hering (“herring”), Bavarian Haring (“herring”). Late Latin haringus (whence French hareng, etc.) is borrowed from Germanic.

note: hysteria + -ical。ギリシャ語 hystera（子宮）。昔、子宮の不調が原因と考えられた。「ヒステリックな」→（口語）「ひどくおかしい」。
embedded_source: From hysteric + -al, from Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós, “suffering in the womb, hysterical”), from ῠ̔στέρᾱ (hŭstérā, “womb”).

note: in（否定）+ compatible（両立できる）。com + pati（耐える・感じる）。「共に耐えられない」→「両立しない」。patient と同じ。
embedded_source: Borrowed from French incompatible.

note: ラテン語 injunctio（命令）から。in + jungere（結びつける）。「（義務を）課すこと」→「差し止め命令」。junction と同じ。
embedded_source: From Middle English iniunccyon, iniunccion, from Old French injonctïon, from Latin iniūnctiō (“command, injunction”).

note: in（中に）+ nat（生まれる）+ e。生まれつき中にある →「生まれつきの・先天的な」。

More at ramble.

note: ギリシャ神話で歌声で船乗りを惑わすセイレーン（Seirēn）から。人を引きつける音 →「サイレン」。
embedded_source: From Middle English siren, from Old French sereine and Latin Sīrēn, Sīrēna, from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn). The mammalian sense was first attested in French in Dominique Bouhours, Les entretiens d'Ariste et d'Eugène, in 1671. The aquatic salamander sense was originally introduced by Linnaeus in 1766, for a genus of his reptiles.

embedded_source: From Middle English bede (“a prayer”), also “a bead for counting prayers” in a peire of bedes (literally “a pair of beads”), from Old English bedu, bed, ġebed (“a request, entreaty, prayer”), from Proto-West Germanic *bedu, *bed, *gabed, from Proto-Germanic *bedō, *bedą.\nCognate with Saterland Frisian Gebäd (“prayer”), Cimbrian gapéet (“prayer”), Dutch gebed and bede (“prayer”), German Gebet (“prayer”), Low German Gebett (“prayer”), Luxembourgish Gebiet (“prayer”), Vilamovian gybāt (“prayer”).

embedded_source: The noun is derived from Late Middle English birth (“(nautical) bearing away or off, clearance, berth”). Further etymology uncertain, but probably from beren (“to carry (away), bear”) + -th (suffix denoting a condition, quality, state of being, etc., forming nouns); if so, the English word is analysable as bear + -th (suffix forming nouns from verbs), and is a piecewise doublet of birth.\nThe verb is derived from the noun.

embedded_source: From black + mail (“a piece of money”). Compare Middle English blak rente (“a type of blackmail levied by Irish chieftains”).\nThe word is variously derived from the tribute paid by English and Scottish border dwellers to border reivers in return for immunity from raids and other harassment. This tribute was paid in goods or labour, in Latin reditus nigri (“black mail”); the opposite is blanche firmes or reditus albi (“white rent”), denoting payment by silver.\nMcKay derives it from two Scottish Gaelic words blàthaich, pronounced (the th silent) bl-aich, "to protect" and màl (“tribute, payment”)

embedded_source: Borrowed from Spanish junta (literally "a thing gathered or joined"), feminine form of junto, from Latin iunctus, perfect passive participle of iungō (“join”). Attested from 1623.

note: 古英語 læccan（つかむ）から。「掛け金」→「しがみつく（latch onto）」。
embedded_source: From Middle English lacchen (“to seize, catch, grasp”, verb), from Old English læċċan (“to grasp, take hold of, catch, seize”), from Proto-Germanic *lakjaną, *lakwijaną, *lakkijaną (“to seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂g-, *(s)leh₂gʷ- (“to take, seize”). embedded_source: From Middle English libel, from Old French libelle, from Latin libellus (“petition”, literally “booklet”). Doublet of libelle.

note: ラテン語 ligamentum（ひも）から。ligare（結ぶ）。「靱帯」。league と同じ lig。
embedded_source: From Middle English ligament, from Latin ligāmentum, from ligō (“tie, bind”).

note: like（似ている）+ -ness。「類似・肖像」。
embedded_source: From Middle English liknesse, from Old English līcness, ġelīcnes (“the quality of being like or equal; likeness; image; copy; pattern; example; parable”), from Proto-West Germanic *galīkanassī (“likeness”), equivalent to like + -ness.\nCognate with West Frisian likenis (“likeness”), Dutch gelijkenis (“similarity; likeness; parable”), German Low German Glieknis (“form; semblance; likeness; parable”), German Gleichnis (“form; semblance; image; likeness; parable; simile”). The verb is derived from the noun. Compare also Old Norse líkneskja (“figure, image, appearance, likeness”).

note: loft（屋根裏・高い所）+ -y。「高くそびえる」→「高尚な」。lift と同系。
embedded_source: From Middle English lofty, lofti, lofte (“of high rank; noble; ornate”), equivalent to loft (“sky, firmament; upper room”) + -y.

note: 「ぼんやり現れる」は語源ははっきりしない。「織機」は古英語 gelōma（道具）からで別語。
embedded_source: From Middle English lome, from Old English *lōma, ġelōma (“tool, utensil, implement, article of furniture, household effect”) (also as andlōma, andġelōma, andlama (“utensil, instrument, implement, tool, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *lōmō, *lamō (“tool, utensil”), of uncertain origin. Cognate with Dutch alaam, allaam (“tool, household ware or good, appliance”), from Middle Dutch andlame. Perhaps originally meaning "a thing of frequent use, thing repeatedly needed", in which case, akin to Old English ġelōme (“often, frequently, continually, repeatedly”), from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *lōmiz,

note: ラテン語 ludicrus（遊びの）から。ludus（遊び）。「ばかげた」。illusion、elude と同じ lud。
embedded_source: Learned borrowing from Latin lūdicrus. First attested in 1619.

note: スペイン語 maíz から。カリブのタイノ語 mahiz に由来する。「トウモロコシ」。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Spanish maíz, from Taíno *mahis, *mahisi, from Proto-Arawak *marikɨ. Cognate with Lokono marisi, Wayuu maiki.

note: ラテン語 malitia（悪意）から。malus（悪い）。「悪意」。malicious と同じ。
embedded_source: From Middle English malice, borrowed from Old French malice, from Latin malitia (“badness, bad quality, ill-will, spite”), from malus (“bad”).

note: marginalize（周縁に追いやる）+ -ed。margin（縁）。「社会の周縁に追いやられた」。
mix（混ぜる）+ tape。お気に入りの曲を集めて録音したもの。
embedded_source: From mix + tape; originally mix tape.\nOriginally referring to a homemade compilation recorded onto a cassette tape and circulated informally, especially within hip-hop culture, mixtape has broadened in sense. In contemporary usage it often denotes a musical project released outside the conventional album framework, typically characterized by looser structure, experimental material, or informal distribution, even when no physical tape medium is involved.

note: ラテン語 munitio（防備）から。munire（守りを固める）。ammunition と同じ。
embedded_source: From Latin mūnitiō (“a defence, fortification”) via French munition, from mūnīre (“fortify, defend (with a wall)”) + -tiō, from moenia (“city walls, defensive walls, or walls in general”). Equivalent to munite + -ion.

note: 性別を明かさない人のための敬称。Mr. / Ms. にならって作られた。
embedded_source: Coined based on Mr and Ms, with x chosen as a "wildcard" character. First proposed jokingly in print in 1977.

note: ギリシャ語 myrtos から。「ギンバイカ」。
embedded_source: From Middle English mirtille, from Old French mirtille, mirtile, from myrte, from Latin myrtillus, from myrtus + -illus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).

note: relative（相対的な）+ -ity。re + latus（運ばれた）。「相対性」。

note: ラテン語 in limbo（縁に）から。limbus（縁）。天国と地獄の境 →「どっちつかずの状態」。踊りのリンボーは別語。
embedded_source: The noun is derived from Middle English limbo, lymbo (“place where innocent souls exist temporarily until they can enter heaven”), from Latin limbō, the ablative singular of limbus (“border, edge; hem; fringe, tassel”) (notably in expressions like in limbō (“in limbo”) and e limbō (“out of limbo”)); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lemb- (“to hang limply or loosely”), from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang down loosely (?)”). Doublet of limp.\nThe verb is derived from the noun.

note: 古英語 lengan（長引かせる）から。long と同系。「ぐずぐず残る」。
embedded_source: From Middle English lengeren, frequentative of lengen (“to stay, dwell, tarry”), from Old English lenġan (“to lengthen, delay, extend”), from Proto-West Germanic *langijan, from Proto-Germanic *langijaną (compare West Frisian lingje (“to linger”), Dutch lengen, German längen, Icelandic lengja (“to lengthen”)), related to the root of English long. Equivalent to linge or long + -er (frequentative verb suffix).

note: louse（シラミ）+ -y。「シラミだらけの」→「ひどい」。
embedded_source: From Middle English lousy, lowsy, lousi, equivalent to louse + -y.

note: lunch の古い形とされる。「（正式な）昼食会」。
embedded_source: Of uncertain origin. Possibly derived from an earlier *lumpchin, *lumpchen, a diminutive of lump (“chunk, parcel of food, lunch”), thus related to lunch. It is unclear which came first: whether lunch is a shortening of luncheon, or whether luncheon is an augmentation of lunch. Possibly also a dissimilatory form of or influenced by nuncheon (“light snack taken in the afternoon”).\nNoun sense 2 (“sausage”) is likely a ellipsis of luncheon sausage or luncheon meat.

note: ラテン語 memorabilis（記憶すべき）の複数形。「記念品」。memory と同じ。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Latin memorābilia (“things to be remembered”); its use as noun is after Ancient Greek ἀπομνημονεύματα (apomnēmoneúmata) of the neuter plural of memorābilis (“memorable”). Its English use is perhaps after the Latin title Memorabilia of Xenophon’s collection of Socratic dialogues.

note: ギリシャ語 ōidē（歌）から。「頌歌」。melody、parody と同じ。
embedded_source: From Middle French ode, from Late Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”). Doublet of Aoede.

note: 古フランス語 overt（開いた）から。ラテン語 aperire（開く）。「公然の」。covert（隠れた）と対。
embedded_source: From Middle English overt, uverte (“open, uncovered; unfastened; accessible, unobstructed; clear, manifest”), from Anglo-Norman overt, Middle French ouvert, Old French overt, ouvert, uvert (“opened”) (modern French ouvert), past participle of Anglo-Norman, Old French ovrir, ouvrir, uvrir (“to open”), from Late Latin operire, variant of Latin aperīre (“to open”), from aperiō (“to open, uncover”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“away; from”) + *h₂wer- (“to cover, shut”). The English word is a doublet of apert and ouvert.

embedded_source: From Paisley, Renfrewshire, in Scotland, where shawls of this kind were woven in the 1800s.

note: ペルシャ語 pāy（脚）+ jāma（衣服）。インドの「ゆったりしたズボン」→「パジャマ」。
embedded_source: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi पाजामा (pājāmā) / Urdu پاجامہ (pājāma)), from Classical Persian پَاجَامَه (pājāma, “trousers, drawers”), from پَا (pā, “leg”) + جَامَه (jāma, “garment”).

note: ギリシャ語 patēr（父）+ arkhēs（長）。「家長・長老」。monarch と同じ arch。
embedded_source: From Middle English patriark, patriarche, from Late Latin patriarcha; later reinforced by Old French patriarche, from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -ᾰ́ρχης (-ắrkhēs, “-arch”), with some senses likely influenced directly by Latin pāter (“father”) or Ancient Greek πᾰτήρ (pătḗr, “father”). Compare matriarch. By surface analysis, patri- + -arch.

note: 古フランス語 apentis（差しかけ小屋）から。append と同系。house に結びつけられた。「最上階の高級住宅」。
embedded_source: From Anglo-Norman pentiz (“pentice”), from apendiz (“appentice”), ultimately from a suffixed form of Latin appendō (“to append”). Altered by folk etymology to appear to be a compound of house. Doublet of appentice and pentice.

note: ラテン語 perjurium（偽りの誓い）から。per（悪く）+ jurare（誓う）。「偽証」。jury と同じ jur。
embedded_source: From Anglo-Norman perjurie, from Latin perjūrāre (“swear falsely”), from per- + jūrāre. Displaced native Old English mānāþ (literally “false oath”).

Compare West Frisian wikedei (“weekday”), Dutch weekdag (“weekday”), German Low German Wekendag (“weekday”), German Wochentag (“weekday”), Danish ugedag (“weekday”), Swedish veckodag (“weekday”), Norwegian ukedag (“weekday”), Faroese vikudagur (“weekday”), Icelandic vikudagur (“weekday”).

Compare also Middle English runkel (“wrinkle”), from Old Norse hrukka (“wrinkle”), from Proto-Germanic *hrunkwǭ (“wrinkle, crease”), whence also French fronce (“crooked smile, scowl, frown”), German Runzel (“wrinkle”), Danish rynke (“wrinkle”), Swedish rynka and rynkla (“wrinkle”).

Fōrmātus is the perfect passive participle of fōrmō (“to form, to shape”), from fōrma (“a form, shape”); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a form, shape”) (see further at that entry). By surface analysis, form + -ative.

note: 中英語 hoveren から。「空中に浮かぶ」→ 画面上でマウスを「合わせる」。hovercraft。

The English word is analysable as hove (“(obsolete) to remain suspended, float, hover; to linger, wait”) + -er

on（〜に接して）。お金・時間を〜に「つぎ込む」。spend time doing（〜して時間を過ごす）。
up to（〜まで）+ date（日付）。「今日の日付まで追いついた」→「最新の」。out of date の対。
from（〜から）。「〜から結果として生じる」。result in（〜という結果になる）と方向が逆。
after（後を追って）。親の後を追って同じになる →「（親に）似ている」。
fond（愛着のある）+ of。もとは「ばかなほど好き」。
up（上へ）。気持ちを上向きにする →「元気づける・元気を出す」。
famous（有名な）+ for（〜の理由で）。
